newsitem.title: USA: Sandbags, sweat battle flood in Minnesota town.
newsitem.headline: Sandbags, sweat battle flood in Minnesota town.

text.p: A hand-to-hand human chain hoisting thousands of sandbags was at work Tuesday in this Minnesota village, fighting a spring flood in winter cold.

The scene in Fridley, a town of 28,000 on the Mississippi River north of Minneapolis, was repeated across the northern Midwest this week as a record snowfall melted, fed by a weekend blizzard that dumped still more rain and snow.
Students from Fridley's high school got the day off to help, strengthening the levee system and helping neighbors move their possessions to higher ground.

At a parking lot near the town's municipal garage they worked alongside Civil Air Patrol cadets, city workers and volunteers, turning plastic traffic cones upside down to serve as funnels to get the sand into the bags.
Ken Holmstrom, the city street supervisor overseeing work at the parking lot, said he expectsed another 4,000 bags to be filled by nightfall.
"We will then have a total of 21,000 to 22,000 sandbags since we started last week," he said, adding he hoped that would be enough.

It is cold work. The temperature is 20 degrees Fahrenheit. A raw wind makes it feel much worse. The bags are brought to Riverview Heights Park where people have been working since Friday to build a dike across Spring Brook Creek.
At the park a chain of another 100 high school students and about 75 Civil Air Patrol cadets takes the bags from the trucks to where the dike is being built up.
"The creek is a major problem," said volunteer Al Stahlberg. "The water is trying to get into the Mississippi River, but because the river is so high, there's a danger that the creek will back up."
A shopping center and an industrial park are threatened.

Concrete barriers used to separate highway traffic lanes on the highway have been put on the levee to form the basis of a new dike. The barriers are covered with plastic and then sandbags are piled up in between the barriers.
Scott Robinson, a 15-year veteran of the Fridley police force, has stationed his cruiser on the dike alongside the Mississippi River to keep the road clear for the trucks bringing sandbags.

The river now is almost at the top of the dike built after a record 1965 flood to protect about 20 low-lying homes. It is expected to crest in Fridley some time between Thursday and Friday, by which time the new sandbag defense line should be in place.
But residents of houses right behind the dike have either moved their possessions to the second floor or have already moved out.
"When the whistle blows, sometime in the next couple of days, you will only have a couple of minutes to leave," a man said while he and his friends loaded up a rented truck.

Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson wrote to President Clinton Tuesday for help, suggesting that 21 counties be declared federal disaster areas. So far high water has driven about 5,000 people in Minnesota out of their homes.
